title: Not born, not destroyed
hookLine: all things marked by emptiness: not born, not destroyed, not stained, not pure, not growing, not shrinking

lines: AN ICE CUBE IN A GLASS.
cards: Drop an ice cube into a glass of water and watch. The edges soften. It shrinks.
A minute later there's no ice cube. So when did it die? And where did it go?
Nothing left the glass. The water is a little colder and a little fuller. The cube didn't vanish into nothing, and it didn't come from nothing either: it was water before the freezer got to it.
You'd still say the ice is gone. That's true, and useful. But it isn't the whole story.

teach.b: Avalokiteshvara is still speaking to Shariputra. Having said form is emptiness, he goes on: all things are marked by emptiness. They are not born and not destroyed.
Not stained and not pure. Not growing and not shrinking. Three pairs, six nots.
In Sanskrit the first two are anutpanna, not arisen, and aniruddha, not ceased. Here's the thread. Two days ago: nothing stands alone, everything is made of causes and conditions.
If that's true, nothing starts from zero. A tree was a seed, the seed was a tree, and both were rain and soil and sun.

And nothing ends at zero: a fallen tree becomes soil for the next one. Birth and death are real names for real changes, a shift in conditions, not something popping in or out of existence. Same with stained and pure.
Dirt isn't a fixed essence stuck to a thing, and neither is cleanness.

Mahayana teachers explain this with two truths. At the everyday level, people are born, people die, and grief is honest. At the deepest level, they say, nothing has a separate self that could be born or destroyed.
Both are true at once, and the point is never to tell a grieving person the loss isn't real. The sutra itself, well-known for being short, explains none of this.
The explanations come from commentators in India, China and Tibet, and they don't all agree on the details. What they share is the direction: look closely at an ending, and you find a change.

how: Mahayana Buddhists in East Asia, Tibet and beyond chant the Heart Sutra's line about things being not born and not destroyed in daily services and at funerals, and teachers explain it through the two truths.

o: lasting forever, with no change at all
doesn't come from nothing; it changes
never existed in the first place

games.q: match each pair in the Heart Sutra's line.

s: the Heart Sutra says nothing ever changes
it says things don't start from nothing or end in nothing; change is exactly what it points at.
the sutra lists three pairs of 'nots'
not born, not destroyed; not stained, not pure; not growing, not shrinking.
Mahayana teachers use two truths to explain the line
everyday birth and death are real; at the deepest level nothing has a separate self to be born.

games.q: a friend whose grandmother just died has heard the Heart Sutra line. she asks you: so it's saying she didn't really die? what do today's teachers say?
o: yes, so there's nothing to grieve.
her death is real at the everyday level; the line points at what she was made of and passed on.
the sutra is only about ice and trees, not people.
games.why: Mahayana teachers hold two truths at once: the loss is real and grief is honest, and at the deepest level nothing had a separate self that could vanish into nothing.

practice: Let the breath come in on its own, and notice where it was a moment ago: outside you, part of the room; now inside, warm; then out again, the room once more. When did it begin, and when does it end?
No answer needed; just watch the air change places, and if a thought appears, notice that it too came from somewhere and goes somewhere.

wordCard.voice: Not born. Anutpanna, not arisen: in the Heart Sutra, things marked by emptiness don't start from nothing or end in nothing. They change.

orig.note: Sanskrit anutpanna: not arisen, unborn; the Heart Sutra pairs it with aniruddha, not ceased.

carryVoice: Your line: no birth, no death. Not a denial of loss, but a closer look at change. That's day two hundred seventy-one.

sources.work: Nagarjuna, Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way
